planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into moist to seasonally flooded, brackish to saline sandy or silty soil in full sun; marsh fimbry occupies the high marsh zone along the Gulf and South Atlantic coasts, just above the reach of most tides, and establishes best where soil stays damp but is not permanently submerged.

directions: Set divisions into moist to periodically flooded, brackish to saline sandy or silty soil in full sun along the upper edges of tidal marshes, brackish ditch banks, or salt-influenced low spots in coastal landscapes. Marsh fimbry forms tight, grass-like tufts of wiry, dark green foliage topped in summer by small chestnut-brown seed clusters that give the plant its species name, and it is one of relatively few native sedges that tolerates the salinity of the high marsh zone without losing vigor. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes to knit together bare, salt-stressed soil, making it useful for stabilizing marsh-edge plantings, tidal creek banks, and brackish rain garden margins where turfgrass and most ornamental sedges fail. Once established it needs no fertilizer and tolerates both periodic tidal wetting and drier interludes between spring tides.

planting.note: Plant rooted runners or plugs in spring into loose, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to light shade on dunes, back-dune swales, or sandy coastal ground; largeleaf pennywort is a true dune and beach-front species, distinct from the wetter, pond-margin marsh pennywort (Hydrocotyle umbellata).

directions: Plant in loose, well-drained sand in full sun to light shade along dunes, back-dune flats, and sandy coastal edges; largeleaf pennywort spreads by long, trailing runners that root at the nodes, sending up rounded, umbrella-like leaves on individual stalks to form an open, low groundcover across bare sand. It tolerates salt spray, occasional overwash, and drought once established, helping to knit loose dune sand together alongside sea oats and railroad vine without competing aggressively for space. Small greenish flower clusters appear on short stalks through the warm season and are visited by a range of small pollinators, though the plant is grown mainly for its dune-stabilizing habit rather than for bloom. Avoid rich soil or regular irrigation, both of which favor weedier competitors over this sand-adapted native.

planting.note: Set container-grown plants in fall or spring into well-drained sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade along maritime forest edges, coastal scrub, or brackish marsh borders; silverling tolerates salt spray and periodic brackish flooding but, unlike its relative Baccharis halimifolia, prefers slightly better-drained ground.

directions: Plant in well-drained sandy or loamy soil in full sun to part shade along maritime forest margins, coastal hammocks, or the upper, less frequently flooded edges of brackish marshes. Silverling is a rounded, semi-evergreen shrub closely related to the more common sea myrtle (Baccharis halimifolia) but generally more compact and tolerant of slightly drier, better-drained coastal soils, making it a useful companion planting where the ground does not stay saturated. Female plants produce the same characteristic silvery-white seed tufts in fall that give the species its common name, offering late-season texture and supporting overwintering songbirds that feed on the fluffy seed heads. It tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil with no supplemental fertilizer once established, and responds well to occasional pruning to maintain a dense form in foundation or screening plantings near the coast.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into saturated to shallowly flooded, fresh to slightly brackish soil in full sun along the margins of bayous, tidal creeks, and freshwater-to-brackish transition marshes; giant cutgrass spreads aggressively by rhizome and needs ample room.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions into saturated soil or shallow standing water in full sun along the edges of bayous, tidal freshwater and brackish marshes, or large pond margins with room to spread. Giant cutgrass forms tall, coarse-textured stands of broad, sharp-edged leaf blades that dominate the transition zone between freshwater and brackish coastal marshes across the Gulf Coast, providing dense cover for rails, gallinules, and other marsh birds as well as nursery habitat for young fish and crustaceans along tidal creek edges. Because it spreads vigorously by thick rhizomes and can quickly colonize open shoreline, it is best used in large-scale wetland restoration or expansive water-garden settings rather than small residential ponds, and it should be kept well away from open irrigation or drainage channels where it could spread unchecked. It requires no fertilizer and thrives on the natural nutrient load of marsh and bayou-edge water once established.
